title: Chapter 128 – The Southern Road
html:
[Southern Road – Lin Jian]

The Nameless follows them for eleven days, and never once closes the distance.

Jian counts. It is a habit he cannot break. On the first day the figure is forty paces behind the last wagon; on the second, forty again; on the third, forty. He walks when the caravan walks and stops when it stops. At night, while the Tan guards light their cook-fires and sing their dull, comfortable marching songs, he sits cross-legged in the road at the edge of the lantern light and does not eat, does not drink, and does not appear to sleep.

By the fourth day the guards have stopped pointing at him. By the sixth, they have given him a nickname. The Shadow. By the eighth, a young drover named Xu Dai leaves a bowl of rice at the forty-pace line each evening, as one might for a stray dog, and every morning the bowl is empty and clean and set exactly where it was.

Yue watches him from the wagon with her ledger on her knee.

"He is not alive," she says, on the eleventh day.

"He is."

"He is not quiet." She frowns at the page. "Everything alive makes a seam. A small one. The breath in and out, the heartbeat, the blink. Pebble can hear them all. A cart horse sounds like a spinning wheel. A man sounds like a drum." She taps the pencil on her teeth. "He sounds like nothing. Like a stone someone has hollowed out and set in the road."

"He is a Number. They are made that way."

"Then why does he follow us?"

Jian has been asking himself the same question for eleven days. He has no answer. He has a suspicion, and it is the sort of suspicion that does not improve with attention.

"I am going to ask him," he says.

* * *

The days between are the plain days of the road, and he finds, to his surprise, that he likes them.

He earns his CE the old way, by labor. It is slow, and it is honest. In the evenings, when the wagons circle and the guards sit down to eat, he takes his place at the end of the fire beside the drovers and asks whether anything wants mending. There is always something. A cracked axle-pin. A split yoke. A saddle-strap rubbed through to the last thread. He sits in the lamplight with a borrowed awl and a coil of waxed cord, and the work goes into his hands with the quiet, absorbed satisfaction of a task that is exactly the size of the man doing it.

At the end of each night, a small warm thing settles under his breastbone. Two units. Two, no more. He has tested it on the second night, and the fourth, and the seventh; it never varies. Two for a night's honest work, six for a week, and nothing at all for a night he spends idling. It is, he thinks, the most reasonable bargain the thing in his head has ever offered. It asks only that he be useful.

"You are very good at that," says Xu Dai, the young drover, watching him sew a harness. He is nineteen, with a cleft chin and a worried brow, and he leaves the bowl of rice at the forty-pace line every evening without being asked.

"I had a long apprenticeship."

"In what?"

Jian considers. "Gardens," he says.

"Gardens do not teach you to do that."

"They teach you that everything wants to be put back the way it was." He pulls the cord tight and bites it off. "The rest is knots."

The boy laughs. Down the line, in the wagon, Yue is writing, with Pebble curled on the page. Over the Kettle the first stars are coming out, hard and bright in the dry cold air, and Jian lifts his head from the harness and finds himself naming them, one by one, under his breath. Hearth. Ladle. The Weaver's Girl. He knows them all. He is startled, every time, by how much he knows.

He is also quietly aware of what he does not. Somewhere in the dark of his mind there is a small round hole, the shape of a word, and he walks around it every evening as a man walks around a well.

* * *

He walks back along the road at dusk, alone, with the red sun behind him.

The caravan has halted at a dry ford, in a wide stony valley, and the guards are setting a ring of wagons. Smoke rises. Somebody is tuning a fiddle. He leaves all of it behind him at an easy walk, with his hands loose and his short robe flapping, and in a hundred paces the sound is gone and there is only the creak of cooling stone, and a last bird, and the dry rustle of wind in thorn-bush.

The Nameless sits in the middle of the road with its legs crossed and its palms on its knees, exactly where it sat yesterday.

Jian stops six paces off. He has never seen it up close. In the red light it is merely a thin man in plain gray, with close-cropped hair and ordinary hands. The face is the trouble. His eyes slide off it. He looks at the nose and finds himself thinking of the sky. He looks at the mouth and thinks of a locked door. It is not a mask; there is nothing to lift. It is simply a face that has been taken, a piece at a time, until nothing is left for the memory to hold.

"You have been following us," says Jian.

"Yes."

The voice is level, quiet, pleasant. A clerk's voice.

"Why?"

"I was asked to see that you reach the first Dock alive."

"By whom?"

"I do not know." The head tilts a fraction. "That is the difficulty. I was told, and the telling is still in me, and the one who told me is not. The Roll closed its mouth, you understand. The Keeper burned her name. What I carry now is a message with no sender, and I have no way to ask what it meant." A faint, dry pause. "I am obliged to follow it anyway. It is, after all, all that I have."

Jian considers this.

"You offered me a seat," he says. "At the Gate stair. A year ago."

"I did."

"I declined."

"You did." The Nameless inclines its head, courteously. "I record that I was not offended. I record that you were, in my judgment, wise. A seat in the House is a fine thing to be offered and an extraordinarily poor thing to accept." Another pause. "I was a Number for forty-one years. I do not recommend it."

"What was your name?"

"I do not know."

"Do you want to?"

For the first time, something moves under the surface of the voice. A slight stiffening. A held breath. "Is that an offer?"

"I do not have your name. Elder Ye has a list. She is reading from it. She has restored one man in a month, and she says there are four thousand."

"Four thousand and some."

"You know the number."

"I helped to keep it." The Nameless looks at its own hands. "It is an odd feeling, to be a ledger. To be the thing a count is made of. I do not think I have ever said that aloud." It lifts its eyes, and for an instant, a half-instant, Jian has the dizzying sense of a real face behind the blank one, a lined, tired, middle-aged face pressed against the inside of the glass. "No. I do not want my name. Not yet."

"Why not?"

"Because I do not trust what I would be, when it came back."

The wind rises. A dry thorn rolls across the road between them, caught on nothing.

"I will say one more thing," says the Nameless softly, "and then I will be quiet. There are others behind me. Not the House. The House has withdrawn, and meant it. These are the ones who were not on the roll when the Keeper died. The ones who had been burned, and kept, and let go, and who have no one now to hold them." The head turns slowly toward the south. "They are not like me. They have been given the message too. But they have not been given the courtesy."

"What message?"

"That the eighth is on the road."

* * *

On the thirteenth night, Yue teaches Pebble to count.

It is her own idea. She sits cross-legged in the wagon bed under a hooded lantern with the little gray beast in front of her and a handful of dried beans on the board between them, and she lays them out in rows. One. Two. Three. She says each number aloud, slowly, in the clear patient voice she uses for the ledger, and Pebble repeats it after her in that strange high child's voice that seems to come from somewhere other than her throat.

"Seven," says Pebble.

"Good."

"Seven is a seam."

"Seven is a number."

"Seven is a number that is a seam." The little beast considers the beans with her head on one side. "When a thing is counted, it can be held. When it cannot be counted, it slides. That is what a seam is. Where the counting stops."

Yue stops with a bean between her fingers. "Say that again."

"Where the counting stops." Pebble lifts her eyes. They are two flat, dull coins in the lantern light, and for a moment they look very old. "I did not know the words until you taught me the numbers. Now I do. A seam is where one thing ends and the next thing has not begun. There is a gap. In the gap, there is nothing. Nothing is a thing that cannot be counted." She pauses. "That is why he steps there. It is the only place where the road does not need a count."

Jian, sitting at the wagon's tail with the harness in his lap, has gone very still.

"Who taught you that?" he asks.

"No one. You did." The little head turns. "When you stepped into the air today. The Door said it. I only heard."

"The Door said it."

"In its own words. Not mine." Pebble blinks slowly. "It talks, Jian. Not in sentences. In the shape of a sentence. The way a cloak holds the shape of the man who wore it."

Yue lays the bean down very gently, as though it might break. Neither of them speaks. Out in the dark the Nameless is a dim gray shape at the edge of the lantern light, utterly still, and over the Kettle the stars wheel on, patient and enormous, the same stars that were there when the Gate was built.

"I think," says Pebble, "that the Door knows who it was made for."

"And who is that?"

The little beast looks at him for a long time.

"I think you should ask it," she says. "On the other side."

The caravan is attacked on the fourteenth day.

Jian has been expecting trouble, and so has everyone else. The southern road runs through the Kettle, a long dry basin of salt and scrub and broken stone, and every drover on it will tell you the same story: that there are men in the Kettle who will take your cargo, your oxen, your wife and your life, in that order, and thank you for the trouble. Tan Bo has hired thirty guards for a reason. He has also, quietly, hired two Foundation Establishment men on the side, and Jian has seen them watching the ridge-lines with their hands on their swords since noon.

It happens at the ford.

There is a river here, wide and shallow and brown, running over flat red rocks. The caravan crosses it in file, wagon by wagon, with the guards wading beside the oxen. Jian is in the middle, with his boots off and Yue's pack on his back, and Pebble perched on the barrel in front of him. He is thinking about nothing. He is calculating the number of nights it will take him to earn thirty CE by mending harness.

Pebble's head comes up.

"Left," she says.

She says it in her clear child's voice, calmly, as one might say it is raining. Yue, behind him, looks up.

"What?"

"Left. Up. In the rocks." The little beast's ears are flat. "Eleven of them. One is loud."

Jian does not wait to ask. He drops Yue's pack, takes her by the shoulder with one hand, and shoves her down behind the nearest wagon wheel. And as he does it the first arrow comes whistling out of the red cliff and lands in the bed of the wagon where her head had been.

The Kettle erupts.

* * *

They come down the rocks like locusts, in rags, with salt-whitened faces and curved swords. There are more than eleven. There are forty, fifty, boiling out of the gullies on either side, whooping, throwing hooked ropes over the wagon sides. The Tan guards close ranks, shouting. An ox bellows. A woman screams.

In the middle of it all, standing on top of a boulder with his arms spread like a priest at an altar, is the man Pebble called loud.

He is enormous. Seven feet tall, naked to the waist, with a body like a bundle of cables and a face painted white as a skull. A fat gold ring hangs from one ear. In his right hand he carries a long hooked glaive, and even from here Jian can feel the pressure rolling off him: dense, hot, heavy, the unmistakable weight of Foundation Establishment at its Peak.

"He is a Peak," says Yue breathlessly, at his knee. "Jian. He is a Peak."

"I know."

"The guards cannot hold him."

"I know."

"What do we do?"

He does not know. He has twelve CE in a pouch at his belt and a Seam Needle that costs six and will stop a man for an instant, not for a battle. He has the Hollow Echo, a stick strike that costs no CE, but needs a seam to work, and the ford is flat red stone, as clean as a plate. He has his body, Body Eight, Purple Mansion, a thing built over twenty years of grinding into a frame that can lift a wagon. But the Peak has a glaive and a hundred bandits to cover him. A frontal strike will cost a limb.

Pebble is trembling on the barrel.

"There," she says suddenly.

"Where?"

"Behind him." Her voice is high and tight. "There is a seam. A new one. Big. It runs from the boulder to the river, and it is open."

Jian looks. He sees nothing: air, heat shimmer, red dust.

"I cannot see it."

"No," says the little beast. "You cannot see it. But your door can."

* * *

He does not understand what she means until it is too late to ask.

The pressure in his breastbone, the hum of the Cole door, the held note, rises suddenly like a struck bell. It does not hurt. It widens. He feels it open under his ribs, the way a hand opens, and through the opening comes a sensation that he has felt once before, in the dark, in a cold stone stair, with his palm on the Gate. Not seeing. Knowing. A great flat plane of nothing, ruled across with hairline cracks, each of them a bright thin line of certainty in the red dusk.

He knows where the seams are. All of them.

There is one at the foot of the boulder. A long thin crack, a hand's breadth wide and a hundred paces long, that opens in the air above the ford like a slit in a curtain. He could step into it. He knows that. He knows it the way he knows how to breathe.

Door in Summer, says the part of him that is not afraid. It was always here. You only had to be standing in the right season.

He does not stop to think. He puts one bare foot on the wet stone, steps forward, and walks into the air.

* * *

The world folds.

It is not painful. It is not even strange. There is a sense of passing between two sheets of paper, a thin dry whisper of nothing, a half-second of silence in which he hears Pebble's voice, very small and far away, saying yes, yes, that one, and then he is standing behind the boulder, on cold dry rock, ten paces from the Peak.

The bandit chief has his back to him. He is shouting. He lifts his glaive.

Jian has a stick in his belt. It is Wenyuan's old hoe-handle, ash, a little over arm's length, polished smooth by thirty years of weeding. He draws it. He sets his bare feet. And behind the great scarred back of the man in front of him, he sees, with the cold clarity of the Door, a thin dark line running down the spine of the boulder: the seam in the rock that nobody else has noticed, the weakness in the stone.

He strikes.

It is the Hollow Echo, the first technique he ever invented. A stick, a seam, a note. The tip lands on the line with a sound like a dropped coin, and the whole boulder rings. The glaive-man spins, startled, and the stone beneath his feet splits from end to end, with a crack like a thunderclap, and he drops three feet into the gap with his arms flailing and his weapon flying.

He does not get up.

Jian steps over him and puts the stick across his throat. Nothing in his body hurts. His hands are steady. All around the boulder the bandits have stopped, like puppets with their strings cut, staring at the white-faced giant lying in the rubble with a plain brown stick at his neck.

"Tell them to go," he says.

The man looks up at him. In the painted skull of a face the eyes are astonished. "Who—"

"Tell them to go. Now. Or I will find the next seam, and the one after that."

There is a very long silence. Then the giant opens his mouth and roars a single hoarse word in the Salt Hands' pidgin. The bandits scatter. They go up the cliffs like rain running backwards, and in half a minute the Kettle is empty, except for the dead, and the ox, and the sound of the river.

* * *

They bury eleven that evening: four guards, five drovers, two of the Salt Hands who died in the rocks.

It is done quickly and without speeches, in a hollow above the ford, with flat stones for markers and a tin cup of river water poured on each grave. Xu Dai holds the shovel. He does not weep. He digs, and sets the shovel against his shoulder, and digs again, with the stiff, white-lipped concentration of a boy who has decided that if he stops he will break.

Jian takes the next shovel without a word.

They work side by side in the red light. There is nothing to say. When the last stone is down, Xu Dai wipes his forehead with his sleeve, looks at the line of mounds, and asks in a thin voice, "Do you know the names?"

"Of whom?"

"The dead. Mine. Yours." He swallows. "The Salt Hands'."

"I know yours." Jian straightens. "Zhang Lu. Old Pei. Ruan Mei. Han, the cook's brother. Tuo Xiao." He pauses. "Not theirs. I did not ask."

"Why does it matter?"

It is an honest question. Jian looks at the mounds, at the dry grass, at the tin cup on the last stone with a thin skin of dust already forming on the water.

"Because somewhere," he says slowly, "there is a ledger. And in that ledger, a man can be struck off for dying. Everyone remembers the living. The dead are what we owe." He puts the shovel on his shoulder. "I would like to be a man who knows the names."

Xu Dai does not answer. But that night, when he sets down the rice bowl at the forty-pace line, he sets down a second one beside it, small and plain, with a pair of chopsticks laid across the rim.

In the morning, both are clean.

Tan Bo sits on an overturned barrel and drinks four cups of tea without stopping.

"Fifty," he says. "There were fifty of them. I counted. Fifty men, and every one of them knew, Lin Jian. They knew where the guards were, they knew which wagon carried the silk, they knew the day. There has been no raid on this road in three years. The Salt Hands have been paid not to touch us since my father's time." His plump face is gray. "Someone told them."

"Who?"

"My uncle." He swallows. "My uncle Boren has wanted the southern route since I was a boy. He paid the Registry for seventeen years to keep Ruyan out of the family book, and I think he has decided that a caravan which does not exist is a caravan that cannot be inherited."

"Ruyan is not on this road."

"No. But her cousin is." A wry, trembling smile. "I am the one he cannot afford to leave alive."

The chief of the Salt Hands, trussed and bleeding, is being questioned by two of the Tan guards. He is not saying much. From where Jian sits, wrapping a strip of cloth round his bruised palm, he can see the white-painted face, and the gold ring, and the dull look of a man who has not yet understood what happened to him. He is not a clever man. He has been hired. He has been paid in advance, with a bag of silver stamped with a small blue crane.

The Tan mark.

Not Ruyan's. Not Bo's. A third hand.

Yue is crouched by the river, washing her ledger's cover with a wet rag, with her mouth pressed tight. Pebble lies in her lap, gray and quiet. The little beast has not said a word since the fight.

"Is she hurt?" Jian asks.

"No." Yue does not look up. "She is thinking. She does that now. She goes quiet and her seams go quiet and I have to wait." She wrings the rag. "She says you walked into the air."

"Yes."

"I could hear it. When you did it. A great long note, like a bell being rung in a well." She finally lifts her head. Her face is pale and very serious. "Jian. It was the loudest thing I have ever heard in my life."

He says nothing. He is looking at his own hand, the right one, with the callus along the thumb. It does not look any different. It looks like a hand.

None yet.

He closes the panel. The pouch at his belt is lighter by four. In his breast pocket the little wooden spoon presses warm against his ribs, as if it were reminding him of something he cannot quite remember.

"Pebble," he says.

The little beast opens one eye.

"What did you see?"

"A great many things." Her voice is quiet. "More than I can say. I think the south is not a place. I think it is a field. A field of seams, like grain, all the way to the horizon, and every one of them pointing the same way."

"Which way?"

She turns her head toward the red west, toward the setting sun and the long dry road running down into the dusk.

"Down," says Pebble.
